case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that the harms the asylum applicant suffered—including threats and physical mistreatment—do not amount to “persecution.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the persecution standard) and, as to the standard of review for agency findings in immigration petitions for review, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) (substantial-evidence/conclusive administrative findings rule).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that whether established facts rise to the legal threshold of “persecution” is a legal or at least mixed question that should receive de novo review (or more searching review than substantial-evidence), and that treating this determination as a factfinding effectively insulates inconsistent and error-prone BIA/IJ decisionmaking from meaningful appellate correction, undermining uniformity and accurate application of the asylum statute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government contends that Congress mandated substantial-evidence review for the agency’s determination here; that the “persecution” assessment is a fact-bound application of law to the particular record (not a pure legal question); and that the First Circuit correctly applied deferential review in concluding the record did not compel a finding of persecution under the INA.
key_precedents: Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best counter: that “persecution” is a mixed question and, per Guerrero-Lasprilla and Lakeridge, warrants de novo review to promote uniformity. But Guerrero-Lasprilla construed “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) only to restore jurisdiction and expressly reserved the standard-of-review issue, so it cannot displace Congress’s separate, affirmative directive in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative findings are conclusive unless the record compels the contrary. Even accepting Justice Jackson’s mixed-question framing, Lakeridge’s default approach yields where Congress has specified a review standard, and here the agency’s persecution call is dominated by context-laden, record-specific line-drawing rather than pure statutory meaning. A narrow disposition can preserve de novo review for articulating the legal standard of persecution while applying Elias-Zacarias and § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s compelled-to-conclude framework to the agency’s application on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s mixed-question and uniformity argument (invoking Lakeridge and Loper Bright) is the strongest, but it cannot overcome the INA’s specific textual allocation in § 1252(b)(4)(B): agency factfinding is “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” which by its terms governs the record-bound application here. Justice Sotomayor is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla treats some applications of law to fact as “questions of law,” but—as Justice Gorsuch and the Chief Justice stress—that case interpreted § 1252(a)(2)(D) for jurisdictional access and expressly reserved the distinct standard-of-review issue, so it does not displace Congress’s separate directive in (b)(4)(B). On an original public meaning reading of the 1996 scheme, Congress codified the substantial-evidence/compulsion framework reflected in Elias-Zacarias, preserving de novo review for the legal meaning of “persecution” while requiring deference to the agency’s ultimate on-this-record line-drawing absent compelled error. Loper Bright restores independent judicial judgment on statutory meaning, but it does not license courts to rewrite a clear statutory standard of review into de novo reassessment of fact-intensive eligibility determinations.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s uniformity and mixed-question framing (via Lakeridge) is the strongest argument for de novo review, but it cannot overcome Congress’s specific instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that agency findings are conclusive unless the record compels a contrary result; whatever “persecution” is in the abstract, this determination is inseparable from the granular record assessment Congress chose to insulate from appellate reweighing. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla usefully shows that some applications of law to fact can be “questions of law” for jurisdictional access, but as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, Guerrero-Lasprilla expressly did not set the standard of review and did not construe (b)(4)(B), so it does not displace the INA’s explicit deferential review regime. Elias-Zacarias—and Congress’s codification of that approach—confirms that reversal is appropriate only when the evidence compels the opposite conclusion, while courts remain free to correct de novo any legal misstatement of the persecution standard. Loper Bright eliminates Chevron on pure statutory meaning, but it does not authorize courts to reclassify record-bound applications as de novo legal questions where Congress has mandated deference.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s best point is that Guerrero-Lasprilla was jurisdictional and did not itself “set the standard of review,” and I agree it cannot simply be transplanted wholesale; but it still illuminates the classification problem at the center of § 1252(b)(4)(B)—whether the ultimate persecution determination is truly a “finding of fact” or an application of a legal standard to found facts that demands meaningful judicial supervision. Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan lean heavily on Elias-Zacarias and say Congress “codified” that deferential approach, yet Elias-Zacarias involved substantial-evidence review of motive and did not hold that the legal threshold for what counts as persecution is itself insulated from de novo correction when the facts are settled. My concern remains that treating the persecution label as conclusive factfinding invites systemic under-protection through inconsistent, record-bound line-drawing that disproportionately harms vulnerable applicants, while de novo review of the persecution determination can be cabined to the agency’s found facts and credibility findings and thus need not become appellate reweighing. Loper Bright, as Justice Gorsuch notes, does not speak directly to § 1252(b)(4)(B), but it reinforces that courts must exercise independent judgment on legal components absent a clear command—and I do not read (b)(4)(B) as clearly reclassifying this mixed legal application as unreviewable “fact.”

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s Lakeridge-based point—that “persecution” is a mixed question warranting de novo review to promote uniformity—squarely frames the best case for petitioner, but it runs into Congress’s specific allocation in § 1252(b)(4)(B): administrative factfinding is “conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” a directive that pragmatically channels record-bound line-drawing to substantial-evidence review. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla is important for classifying mixed questions as “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D), yet (as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize) that decision expressly did not set a standard of review and cannot displace the separate, affirmative review rule Congress enacted. The coherent middle ground is to preserve de novo review for articulating the legal meaning of “persecution” and correcting legal misstatements, while treating the ultimate “does this record meet that threshold” determination as the kind of context-dependent application Congress meant to be insulated from appellate reweighing under Elias-Zacarias’s compelled-to-conclude framework. Loper Bright reinforces independent judgment on statutory meaning, but it does not authorize us to ignore Congress’s expressly deferential review scheme for record-intensive determinations.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point: that the ultimate “persecution” determination is a mixed question whose legal component should be reviewed de novo to ensure uniformity, drawing on Guerrero-Lasprilla and Lakeridge. But Guerrero-Lasprilla construed “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) only to preserve jurisdiction and expressly declined to prescribe any standard of review, so it cannot displace Congress’s separate, affirmative instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that administrative factfinding is conclusive unless the record compels a contrary result. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Elias-Zacarias reflects the longstanding understanding—later codified—that courts may correct legal misstatements of the persecution standard de novo, yet may not reweigh record-intensive line-drawing absent compulsion; relabeling the agency’s record-bound application as de novo “law” would dilute (b)(4)(B)’s text and invite the very appellate second-guessing Congress sought to curb. Loper Bright does not change this because it concerns who decides statutory meaning in the first instance, not whether courts may ignore an explicit, congressionally prescribed review rule for fact-bound determinations in an administrative record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that “persecution” is a mixed question and that uniformity concerns can favor de novo review under Lakeridge and Guerrero-Lasprilla. But as the Chief Justice stresses, Guerrero-Lasprilla interpreted § 1252(a)(2)(D) for jurisdictional access and expressly did not set a standard of review, so it cannot displace Congress’s separate, explicit review rule in § 1252(b)(4)(B) making administrative factfinding conclusive unless the record compels the contrary. Even accepting the mixed-question label, the predominant work here is record-specific line-drawing—exactly the kind of determination Elias-Zacarias (and Congress’s codification) puts under substantial-evidence/compelled-to-conclude review, while courts remain free to review de novo the legal standard for “persecution” and correct legal errors. Loper Bright does not alter that allocation because we are not deferring to an agency’s statutory interpretation; we are following the review framework Congress prescribed for fact-bound immigration determinations.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the most serious point: that “persecution” is a mixed question and, under Guerrero-Lasprilla and Lakeridge, should receive de novo appellate review to ensure uniformity. But Guerrero-Lasprilla construed “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) for jurisdictional access and expressly left standards of review open; it cannot displace Congress’s separate textual instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that agency findings are conclusive unless a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise. Lakeridge supplies a default framework for mixed questions, yet where (as Justice Roberts emphasizes) Congress has spoken directly to the reviewing court’s role in this specific setting, an originalist/textualist approach gives effect to that allocation rather than importing a generalized standard. Courts still review de novo the legal meaning of “persecution” and correct legal misstatements, but absent such error the record-bound line-drawing remains subject to the codified “compel” standard reflected in Elias-Zacarias.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that § 1252(b)(4)(B) supplies a clear “compelled to conclude” rule and that Elias-Zacarias applied substantial-evidence review, but that only resolves the standard for “findings of fact” and does not answer whether the ultimate persecution determination is properly classified as fact rather than a law-application question. Even accepting their concern about appellate reweighing, Lakeridge’s framework supports de novo review where the work is primarily legal—ensuring a uniform threshold for what counts as “persecution”—while still deferring on historical facts, credibility, and severity details found by the IJ/BIA. Justice Gorsuch is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla was jurisdictional and not a standard-of-review holding, yet it still reinforces that applying a legal standard to settled facts is not itself a pure “finding of fact,” and I do not read § 1252(b)(4)(B) as clearly reclassifying that legal application into conclusive factfinding. Under Loper Bright’s insistence on independent judicial judgment absent clear congressional direction, I remain persuaded that de novo review of the persecution characterization best promotes procedural fairness and nationwide consistency without opening the door to wholesale record reweighing.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and our decision in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), reflects the longstanding understanding that asylum-eligibility determinations are reviewed under that highly deferential standard. Whether a given record of threats and mistreatment rises to the threshold of “persecution” under § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a fact-intensive application of a settled legal standard, and absent a clear congressional signal I would not require across-the-board de novo review that would invite appellate reweighing of the record. Courts of appeals remain free to review de novo the governing legal standard for “persecution,” but the ultimate determination on this record is best treated as predominantly factual under the statutory review scheme. A narrow holding preserving that division of labor respects precedent and promotes institutional legitimacy and uniform administration of immigration law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling text, 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” which calls for substantial-evidence review of the agency’s asylum eligibility determinations on a given record. Consistent with that statute, INS v. Elias-Zacarias applied substantial-evidence review to the BIA’s determination that an applicant was not eligible for asylum and required reversal only when the evidence is “so compelling that no reasonable factfinder could fail” to find persecution. Although identifying the general meaning of “persecution” in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a legal question, whether the particular harms shown in this record meet that standard is a fact-bound application Congress has instructed courts to review deferentially. A de novo standard would improperly displace Congress’s chosen scope of review and expand judicial power beyond the limits set by the statute.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The statutory text directs deferential review: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) provides that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the agency’s determination that particular harms do not rise to the level of “persecution” is a fact-bound application of the INA to a specific record. This Court has repeatedly treated core asylum-eligibility determinations as subject to the “compel” standard, cautioning courts of appeals against substituting their judgments for the agency’s. See INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992) (emphasizing that reversal is warranted only when the evidence compels the opposite conclusion). Whatever Loper Bright did to Chevron, it does not alter Congress’s express command in § 1252(b)(4)(B) or justify turning these record-intensive determinations into de novo appellate review, which would undermine the streamlined, practical administration of immigration law.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Whether proven threats and physical mistreatment rise to the statutory threshold of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is best understood as a mixed question with a substantial legal component that requires meaningful appellate supervision to ensure uniform and fair application of asylum law. Reading 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) to force near-total deference risks insulating inconsistent agency line-drawing on what counts as persecution, with especially severe consequences for vulnerable applicants who may face grave harm if erroneously removed. Guerrero-Lasprilla recognizes that applying a legal standard to established facts is a “question of law” in the immigration context, supporting de novo review of the persecution determination at least insofar as it reflects the application of the legal standard to the record. De novo review here better preserves access to justice and guards against under-protective interpretations of persecution while still respecting the agency’s role in resolving genuine factual disputes.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that "administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary," and the agency’s judgment whether a particular set of harms, in context, crosses the line into "persecution" is predominantly a fact-bound application of the statutory standard in § 1101(a)(42)(A). That structure fits this Court’s long description of asylum-eligibility determinations as reviewed under a substantial-evidence/compelled-to-conclude standard, as reflected in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), and Congress’s 1996 codification of that approach in § 1252(b)(4)(B). While Loper Bright eliminates Chevron deference on pure questions of statutory meaning, it does not undo Congress’s express command of deferential review for factual findings and closely fact-dependent applications embedded in the administrative record. A de novo regime here would be hard to square with § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s text and would invite appellate retrials of persecution severity, reducing workability and undermining the agency’s assigned role as the primary factfinder.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the agency’s persecution determination—whether particular threats and mistreatment on this record cross the statutory line—fits most naturally as a predominantly fact-bound application of the legal standard rather than a freestanding legal interpretation. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr and Wilkinson v. Garland construed the jurisdictional phrase “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) to include mixed questions, but they expressly did not set the standard of review and did not interpret § 1252(b)(4)(B). Consistent with separation-of-powers principles reaffirmed in Loper Bright, courts must decide questions of statutory meaning de novo, but Congress may require deference to agency factfinding, and § 1252(b)(4)(B) supplies that command here. Absent a clearer textual directive from Congress to treat the persecution call as a de novo legal question, I would affirm the First Circuit’s use of substantial-evidence review.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Congress directed that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s persecution determination is best understood as a highly fact-bound application of a general standard to a particular record rather than a freestanding legal interpretation. Our immigration cases have long applied deferential review to the agency’s ultimate asylum determinations, including in INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), which articulated the “compelled to conclude” framework that § 1252(b)(4)(B) codifies. Loper Bright does not alter that statutory command because this is not a Chevron question about deference to an agency’s legal interpretation, but a congressionally prescribed standard for reviewing agency factfinding and fact-intensive judgments. Given precedent, workability, and the need for administrable review that respects Congress’s allocation of responsibility to IJs and the BIA, I would affirm the use of substantial-evidence review here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and the agency’s determination whether the particular harms shown in the record rise to the level of “persecution” under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) is a fact-intensive application of the statutory standard to a specific evidentiary record. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr interpreted “questions of law” in § 1252(a)(2)(D) for jurisdictional purposes and expressly disclaimed resolving the distinct standard-of-review question, so it does not justify converting § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s substantial-evidence framework into de novo review. Consistent with methodological fidelity to Congress’s chosen review rule and this Court’s treatment of asylum eligibility assessments as record-bound, the court of appeals need not apply de novo review to the agency’s no-persecution determination absent a legal error in articulating the standard.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) makes "administrative findings of fact" conclusive unless a reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise, but whether established harms satisfy the statutory standard of "persecution" in § 1101(a)(42)(A) is at least a mixed question requiring courts to articulate and apply uniform legal criteria. Under U.S. Bank Nat’l Ass’n ex rel. CWCapital Asset Mgmt. LLC v. Village at Lakeridge, LLC, the review standard for mixed questions turns on whether resolving the issue entails primarily legal work—here, expounding what kinds of threats and mistreatment qualify as persecution across cases—favoring de novo review. Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo reinforces that courts must exercise independent judgment on legal questions absent a clear congressional directive to defer, and § 1252(b)(4)(B) does not clearly reclassify the persecution determination as a pure factfinding insulated from meaningful appellate correction. De novo review better promotes procedural fairness and consistency in asylum adjudication, while still leaving credibility and historical fact determinations to substantial-evidence review.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a court of appeals must review de novo (rather than for substantial evidence) the agency’s determination that the harms an asylum applicant suffered do not legally amount to “persecution.”
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A) (definition of “refugee,” incorporating the concept of past persecution and well-founded fear); and the INA’s judicial-review framework requiring substantial-evidence review of agency factfinding (commonly applied via 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that whether a given set of established facts rises to the legal standard of “persecution” is a mixed question of law and fact (or a legal characterization) that should not be insulated by deferential substantial-evidence review. They contend that treating “persecution” as a fact question invites inconsistent outcomes, enables unreasoned or overly summary BIA affirmances, and undermines uniform nationwide interpretation of the asylum standard. Several amici (immigration law professors, former EOIR judges, and human-rights scholars) support the view that ‘persecution’ is a legal standard requiring meaningful appellate oversight to ensure consistency and adherence to statutory and international-refugee-law principles.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The government argues the First Circuit applied the correct, congressionally mandated standard: substantial-evidence review of the agency’s determination that the threats and mistreatment alleged here did not rise to the level of persecution. Respondent characterizes the issue as a fact-bound application of a settled legal standard to a highly variable record, the type of determination the INA commits largely to the agency with deferential judicial review. The government also stresses Congress’s choice of substantial-evidence review to promote efficiency and uniformity across very large volumes of asylum cases and argues petitioners’ request would improperly reframe routine, record-specific asylum adjudications as de novo legal questions.
key_precedents: Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024) (mentioned in the government brief excerpt)
INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992) (canonical substantial-evidence standard in asylum review; commonly invoked in this context though not shown in the provided excerpts)
Nasrallah v. Barr, 590 U.S. 573 (2020) (substantial-evidence review for certain agency findings in protection claims; commonly cited in review-standard disputes)
Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021) (limits on judicial reweighing of asylum evidence; often cited regarding deference to agency factfinding)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor (joined in part by Justice Jackson) makes the best point that § 1252(b)(4)(B) speaks to “findings of fact,” and that the legal meaning of “persecution” must remain subject to de novo review to ensure national uniformity. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the run-of-cases “persecution” dispute is not over the governing definition but over whether this record’s degree-and-context facts clear that threshold—an “ultimate fact” determination where de novo review would, in practice, reweigh the record in tension with Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai and with Congress’s compelled-to-conclude scheme. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson (raised by Justice Jackson) confirm that some mixed questions count as “questions of law,” yet they do not compel a categorical de novo rule here; a minimalist approach is to preserve de novo correction for legal-standard mistakes while applying substantial-evidence review to record-bound applications. That narrow division both answers Sotomayor’s reviewability concern and respects the statute’s institutional design and our precedents’ warning against appellate second-guessing.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the persecution label is a mixed question and that de novo review might promote nationwide uniformity, but § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s text makes “administrative findings of fact” conclusive absent compulsion, and the best reading in this statutory setting includes record-bound “ultimate facts” like degree-and-severity judgments. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson, which Justice Jackson invokes, address what counts as a “question of law” for jurisdictional and reviewability purposes, but they do not displace Congress’s specific compelled-to-conclude command when the dispute is whether this record meets a context-dependent threshold rather than what “persecution” means as a matter of law. As the Chief Justice notes, Elias-Zacarias—and as Ming Dai reinforces—warn against appellate reweighing of the evidence in core asylum-eligibility determinations, which is exactly what de novo review of this application step would invite in most cases. De novo review remains appropriate for genuine legal errors about the definition of persecution, but where the agency applies a settled standard to a particular record, substantial-evidence review best matches the statute’s text and structure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s mixed-question framing, echoed by Justice Jackson’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson, highlights a legitimate interest in uniformity, but it does not overcome the INA’s specific instruction that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive” unless the record compels the contrary, § 1252(b)(4)(B). In the run of cases, whether harms rise to “persecution” is not a freestanding legal interpretation but an ultimate, degree-and-context judgment tightly tethered to the evidentiary record—precisely the kind of appellate second-guessing Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai caution against. Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson concern what counts as a “question of law” for jurisdictional access and do not require converting routine, record-bound severity determinations into de novo review where Congress has prescribed a compelled-to-conclude standard. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan suggest, we can preserve de novo review for genuine legal errors about the definition of “persecution” while applying substantial-evidence review to the agency’s application of that standard to particular facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s workability point seriously: de novo review cannot become a backdoor for reweighing severity evidence in a high-volume system, and Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai properly police that boundary. But that concern does not resolve the antecedent interpretive question whether § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s “findings of fact” includes the agency’s application of an open-ended statutory term like “persecution” to established facts; as Justice Jackson notes, Guerrero-Lasprilla and our mixed-question cases treat that application step as having a substantial legal component where de novo review promotes nationwide consistency. I would cabin review to prevent reweighing by accepting substantial-evidence deference on what happened (including credibility and factual severity findings), while preserving de novo correction of the agency’s bottom-line legal characterization when it effectively imposes an unduly restrictive persecution threshold. Justice Thomas’s emphasis on Congress’s allocation to the “trier of fact” in § 1158(b)(1)(B) supports deference on factfinding, but it does not clearly expand § 1252(b)(4)(B) to make the legal minimum for “persecution” functionally unreviewable, especially given the stakes for vulnerable asylum seekers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the textual one: § 1252(b)(4)(B) expressly covers “findings of fact,” and calling “persecution” a legal characterization could advance national uniformity. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, in the INA’s design and our cases (Elias-Zacarias; Ming Dai) the persecution call ordinarily operates as an “ultimate fact”—a record-bound degree/severity judgment—so across-the-board de novo review would, in practice, invite the very reweighing Congress sought to prevent through the “compelled to conclude” standard. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson does affect the analysis by reminding us that some mixed questions are treated as “questions of law,” yet those decisions do not require de novo review of predominantly factual applications where Congress has specified strong deference; they are better read to preserve de novo review for the governing definition/categorical rules while leaving case-specific threshold calls to substantial-evidence review. On a pragmatic textualist approach, that middle ground keeps statutory coherence (meaningful legal oversight without destabilizing high-volume, record-bound adjudication).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual: § 1252(b)(4)(B) names “findings of fact,” and the persecution determination can be described as a legal characterization that benefits from uniform de novo review. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, in this statutory scheme that “persecution” call is ordinarily an ultimate, record-bound severity judgment—precisely the kind of determination Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai treat as reviewable only for whether the evidence compels a contrary conclusion, not for appellate reweighing. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson does not dislodge that result because those cases addressed what counts as a “question of law” for jurisdictional gateways and do not override Congress’s specific, forceful directive in § 1252(b)(4)(B) for reviewing the agency’s record-based determinations. I would still preserve de novo review where the agency misstates the legal definition of persecution or adopts an impermissible categorical rule, but absent that, substantial-evidence review governs the application on this record.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s uniformity/mixed-question point is the best case for de novo review, and Justice Jackson is right that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson treat some applications of law to fact as “questions of law” for certain purposes. But those cases do not displace Congress’s unusually forceful instruction in § 1252(b)(4)(B) that agency factfinding is conclusive absent compulsion, nor our asylum precedents (Elias-Zacarias; Ming Dai) warning courts of appeals not to relabel degree-and-context judgments in order to reweigh the record. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the “persecution” determination here functions as an ultimate fact—predominantly factual in application—and the workable, legitimacy-protecting line is de novo review for the legal definition/categorical rules about persecution, substantial-evidence review for the agency’s record-bound application. I therefore stay with the Respondent while preserving meaningful de novo correction of true legal errors (misstating the persecution standard), which addresses the core of Justice Sotomayor’s reviewability concern without rewriting the statute’s review scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that “persecution” is an application of a legal standard and that mixed questions can warrant de novo review to promote uniformity, as Guerrero-Lasprilla suggests. But § 1252(b)(4)(B) is unusually specific and forceful—making “administrative findings of fact” conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise—and, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the persecution call in the run of cases operates as an “ultimate fact” judgment about degree and context that de novo review would inevitably turn into record reweighing. Justice Jackson’s reliance on Guerrero-Lasprilla/Wilkinson does not displace that statutory command because those cases addressed when mixed questions count as “questions of law” for different jurisdictional provisions, not the INA’s asylum-record review rule keyed to compulsion. Courts still retain de novo authority to correct legal errors about the definition of persecution, but where the dispute is whether this record crosses the threshold, Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai confirm substantial-evidence/compulsion review is the correct mode.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s workability concern is the best argument for Respondent: in a high-volume system, de novo review could become a backdoor for appellate reweighing in tension with Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai. But that concern can be addressed by drawing the line where those cases already draw it—substantial-evidence deference to what happened (and the inferences/credibility determinations that are truly factual), while treating the legal characterization of established harms as meeting the statutory floor of “persecution” as a mixed question with a meaningful legal component under Guerrero-Lasprilla (and the framework Justice Sotomayor advances). Justice Thomas’s reliance on Congress’s references to the “trier of fact” does not, for me, overcome § 1252(b)(4)(B)’s specific limitation to “findings of fact,” especially given the uniformity and procedural-fairness stakes of allowing the agency’s severity threshold to become effectively insulated from judicial correction. I would therefore preserve de novo review for the application of the statutory standard to settled facts, while policing against improper relitigation of disputed facts to respect Congress’s design and the institutional limits Roberts and Kagan identify.

John Roberts.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review framework directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and this Court has repeatedly emphasized that reviewing courts may not reweigh the record in asylum cases. Under INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), substantial-evidence review governs fact-intensive asylum eligibility determinations, and the agency’s application of the persecution standard to a particular record is the sort of case-specific judgment Congress largely committed to the immigration courts. A categorical rule requiring de novo review of the agency’s “persecution” determination risks inviting broader appellate second-guessing inconsistent with Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021), and would undermine institutional legitimacy by destabilizing settled review practices in high-volume adjudication. Consistent with judicial minimalism, I would affirm that substantial-evidence review applies at least where, as here, the dispute concerns the record-bound severity and character of harms rather than a pure legal interpretation of the statutory term.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review command is textual: “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B). Whether the particular harms proved in an individual record rise to “persecution” is predominantly an application of a settled standard to case-specific facts, and thus fits within Congress’s broad phrasing of “findings of fact,” especially given Congress’s repeated designation of persecution/refugee determinations as matters for the “trier of fact,” 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(i)-(ii). This Court has applied substantial-evidence review in asylum determinations and warned courts not to reweigh the record, see INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992), and Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021). Respecting that textually prescribed deference and the agency’s factfinding role, courts of appeals need not (and should not) recast the persecution determination for de novo review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s persecution determination is a fact-bound application of a settled standard to a particular record that Congress assigned primarily to the IJ and BIA. This Court’s asylum cases repeatedly caution courts of appeals against reweighing the evidence and substituting their judgments for the agency’s, see Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021), and apply the substantial-evidence framework in reviewing eligibility determinations, see INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478 (1992). Recasting routine, record-specific persecution assessments as de novo legal questions would invite more appellate second-guessing, undermine the efficiency Congress sought in 1996, and weaken the deference owed to agency adjudications in a high-volume system.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) expressly mandates substantial-evidence review for "administrative findings of fact," but it does not purport to impose deference on the legal characterization of established facts as "persecution" under § 1101(a)(42)(A). Under Pullman-Standard v. Swint, courts distinguish pure facts from mixed questions, and this Court’s mixed-question framework (as reflected in U.S. Bank/Google) calls for de novo review where the task is primarily legal—i.e., elaborating and applying a broad statutory standard in a way that promotes nationwide consistency. Treating "persecution" as effectively a fact question risks insulating unreasoned agency applications of a severe-harm legal threshold, with particularly acute consequences for vulnerable asylum seekers, while still leaving factfinding (including credibility and what happened) to substantial-evidence review consistent with Elias-Zacarias and Ming Dai. De novo review of the persecution determination better ensures uniform application of the refugee definition and meaningful access to justice without authorizing courts to reweigh evidence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(b)(4)(B) directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” and in practice the BIA’s determination that particular threats and mistreatment do (or do not) rise to the level of “persecution” is a highly record-specific application of a settled standard that functions like an “ultimate fact.” INS v. Elias-Zacarias applied substantial-evidence review to the agency’s determination that the applicant failed to carry his burden on a core asylum element, and Ming Dai reinforces that courts may not reweigh such evidentiary determinations on appeal. While courts retain de novo review over the legal meaning of “persecution” as a general standard (and over any legal errors), the workability and volume-driven structure of the INA’s review scheme counsels against recasting routine, fact-bound persecution determinations as de novo questions. Substantial-evidence review thus best fits the statutory text and preserves uniform, administrable appellate review without turning courts of appeals into second-line asylum factfinders.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision commands that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and the agency’s determination whether particular mistreatment rises to the level of “persecution” is, in context, a fact-intensive application of a settled standard rather than an occasion for appellate factfinding. This Court has repeatedly policed the boundary against judicial reweighing in asylum cases under substantial-evidence review, see INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), and more recently in Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021), reinforcing Congress’s allocation of primary responsibility to the IJ and BIA. To require de novo review would invite courts of appeals to substitute their judgment on record-bound assessments Congress assigned to the “trier of fact,” undermining the statutory design and separation of functions reflected in § 1252(b)(4)(B). Whatever the label (“mixed question” or “legal characterization”), the operative inquiry here turns on degree, severity, and context—classic substantial-evidence territory—absent a claim the agency applied the wrong legal definition of persecution under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The INA’s review provision directs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and Congress in 1996 adopted that substantial-evidence framework against the settled backdrop that asylum-eligibility determinations are reviewed deferentially. This Court has repeatedly emphasized that courts of appeals may not reweigh the record in asylum cases and must apply the “compelled to conclude” standard, see INS v. Elias-Zacarias, 502 U.S. 478, 481 (1992), and more recently Garland v. Ming Dai, 593 U.S. 357 (2021). Whether particular mistreatment rises to the level of “persecution” is a highly fact-bound application of a settled legal standard to a variable record, and treating it as categorically de novo would invite appellate relitigation of routine cases and undermine the practical workability Congress sought in this high-volume area. Precedent, statutory text, and institutional considerations therefore support substantial-evidence review of the agency’s persecution determination rather than mandatory de novo review.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The INA’s judicial-review provision instructs that “administrative findings of fact are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B), and this Court has long applied that substantial-evidence framework to the BIA’s asylum-eligibility determinations. INS v. Elias-Zacarias held that a petitioner seeking reversal of the BIA’s determination must show the record evidence is “so compelling that no reasonable factfinder could fail” to find the requisite persecution-related element, treating the agency’s application of the asylum standard to the record as one reviewed deferentially. While “persecution” is a legal term, its application to an applicant’s particular harms is a highly fact-bound, record-specific judgment that Congress has channeled through deferential review to prevent appellate reweighing of evidence, consistent with Garland v. Ming Dai. Given that statutory text and precedent, courts of appeals need not (and should not) impose de novo review for the agency’s persecution determination.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The question whether undisputed or agency-found harms satisfy the INA’s legal standard of “persecution” is an application-of-law-to-fact inquiry that carries a substantial legal component and should receive de novo review to ensure uniformity and procedural fairness in asylum adjudication. The INA’s substantial-evidence command in 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(B) is directed to “findings of fact,” and does not clearly extend to legal characterizations like whether those facts cross the statutory threshold of persecution under 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A). Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr explains that determining whether “a set of facts meets a particular legal standard” is a mixed question, and Wilkinson v. Garland reiterates that mixed questions are treated as questions of law in the INA’s review scheme—supporting meaningful appellate oversight even while courts remain bound by Ming Dai and Elias-Zacarias not to reweigh or second-guess underlying factfinding. De novo review of the persecution characterization better guards against inconsistent, summary BIA dispositions and promotes equal protection values by requiring reasoned, reviewable application of the same legal standard across similarly situated applicants.
